item.description: Separate connector shape, data speed, charging and video support before buying a cable, hub or display.

item.description: Estimate weight storage, then budget explicitly for the runtime and KV cache without claiming that a model will fit or run quickly.

item.description: Read update commitments without inventing a countdown or confusing OS upgrades with security patches.

item.title: Memory market watch: AI demand is not a price quote for your RAM
item.description: Separate company reporting, server-memory products and the delivered price of an exact desktop memory kit.

item.description: Compare exact Canadian configurations, seller support and delivered CAD costs before choosing a gaming desktop.

item.description: A practical US offer checklist for exact desktop SKUs, marketplace sellers, return terms and benchmark context.

item.title: The prebuilt internals checklist: PSU, RAM, cooling and upgrades
item.description: Know which internal details to request before buying a desktop advertised as powerful or upgradeable.

item.title: Phone body size vs screen diagonal: what to compare
item.description: Compare width, height, depth and mass at the same scale instead of treating display inches as hand size.

item.title: Choosing a smaller phone: grip, pockets, case and support
item.description: Build a practical small-phone shortlist around your current device, intended case and remaining support.

item.title: What a 3D PC builder preview can tell you
item.description: Use a model to inspect a build plan while checking dimensions, connectors and clearance in separate evidence.

item.title: Reading a checked PC offer: region, seller, freshness and exclusions
item.description: Understand what an observed hardware price does and does not establish before using it in a buying decision.

item.title: SSD transfer time: why the advertised MB/s is not your copy speed
item.description: Estimate a transfer with the amount of data and a realistic end-to-end rate. An SSD’s advertised sequential read figure describes a particular test; it does not establish how quickly your source, destination, connection and files will complete a copy.

item.title: A new PC has no display: read debug LEDs without guessing the faulty part
item.description: A persistent diagnostic LED helps choose an investigation path. It is not enough, by itself, to justify buying a replacement CPU, memory kit or GPU. Record the exact board and symptom, check the display path, then follow the manufacturer’s safe steps one change at a time.

item.title: RAM compatibility: read the exact kit, slots and QVL evidence
item.description: A QVL records tested memory configurations. A missing entry is a missing validation record, not automatic proof that the kit cannot work. Match generation, kit part number, CPU platform, module count and board instructions before deciding what is supported and what still needs verification.

item.title: Choose a monitor target: verify the output path, refresh rate and game evidence
item.description: Check three different questions: whether the display connection supports the intended mode, whether the operating system is using it, and whether the game can produce useful frames at your chosen settings. A monitor’s maximum refresh rate answers none of the other questions on its own.

item.title: Will a graphics card fit your case? Check the card and cooling layout
item.description: Match the exact graphics-card model to the case as you will install it. Check length, thickness, cable room and radiator placement separately; a passed length check or realistic 3D preview cannot certify the whole fit.

item.title: DDR5-6000 CL30 vs CL36: what the 2 ns calculation can tell you
item.description: At the same 6000 MT/s transfer rate, CL30 corresponds to a calculated 10 ns CAS interval and CL36 to 12 ns. That 2 ns difference is useful specification arithmetic. It is not a measured gaming advantage, a full-system latency result or proof that either profile works on your motherboard.

item.title: Samsung 990 PRO 1 TB vs 870 EVO 1 TB: choose the supported interface
item.description: The 990 PRO 1 TB is an M.2 PCIe/NVMe drive; the 870 EVO 1 TB is a 2.5-inch SATA drive. Choose the model your actual machine can connect and mount, then evaluate the workload and complete cost. Matching capacity does not make these physically or electrically interchangeable.

item.title: AM4 CPU upgrade or AM5 replacement? Compare the whole platform
item.description: An AM4 drop-in candidate can preserve a supported board and DDR4 kit; an AM5 route changes the platform and requires DDR5. Compare complete supported configurations, including keeping the current PC. The CPU price alone cannot establish the cost or usefulness of either upgrade.

item.title: First boot for a new PC: a safe checklist from power-on to a working baseline
item.description: Before installing software or enabling performance profiles, establish that the machine starts, recognizes the intended components and uses a documented configuration. Keep the exact manuals and a short observation log. First boot is a verification sequence, not a race to change every BIOS option.

item.title: Check CPU and BIOS support: exact model, minimum version and update method
item.description: A shared socket is one requirement. Before ordering a CPU, find the exact motherboard support entry, minimum firmware version and a supported way to obtain it. Unknown shipped BIOS is still unknown; an update method available on one board does not establish that another board can use it.

item.title: Plan a phased PC upgrade: make every intermediate build usable
item.description: Buying in stages works only when each intermediate configuration can perform the tasks you still need. Group dependent CPU, board and memory changes, preserve recovery and support evidence, and recheck each later purchase. A future shopping list is not proof that the machine will work between purchases.

item.title: Choose a PC power supply: wattage, connectors, fit and the correct cables
item.description: A wattage label is one requirement, not a complete PSU selection. Check the whole system, exact component connection instructions, physical layout and manufacturer-approved modular cables. Preserve unknowns; matching plugs or a plausible 3D scene do not establish a safe installation.

item.title: RTX 5070 laptop vs desktop: why the name is not the whole comparison
item.description: Compare the complete laptop with the complete desktop. The RTX 5070 Laptop GPU and a desktop RTX 5070 are separate products; the laptop’s exact configuration, graphics power and display matter as much as the short GPU name.

item.title: Can you upgrade a gaming laptop’s RAM and SSD?
item.description: Find the exact laptop model and service manual before buying parts. Some systems have replaceable memory; others have soldered RAM. An SSD upgrade also needs the correct slot, interface, thickness and a plan for your existing files.

item.title: MUX switch vs Advanced Optimus: which laptop setting should you use?
item.description: These features concern the route between the graphics processor and the internal screen. Check what your exact laptop supports, start with its normal recommended mode, and compare one documented change at a time. There is no universal FPS gain.

item.title: Can my PC run Baldur’s Gate 3? Check the requirements before guessing FPS
item.description: Start with the publisher’s requirements for your operating system, including its SSD requirement. Then check exact hardware and relevant game tests. Meeting a requirement does not promise 60 FPS, a particular resolution or the same result throughout the game.

item.title: How to choose a CPU cooler that fits your case and RAM
item.description: Check the exact mounting kit, installed cooler height, RAM clearance and radiator position before buying. Socket support is one check; it does not prove the cooler fits the complete PC or can meet your workload.

item.title: Build vs buy a gaming PC: compare the complete purchase cost
item.description: Compare the exact prebuilt with a complete DIY purchase plan. Include cooling, software, missing accessories and delivery; keep owned parts, checked offers and unknown prices separate.

item.title: How to read GPU benchmarks without comparing the wrong tests
item.description: Compare results only after checking the game, settings, system, capture method and metric. A bigger FPS number can describe a different test. Use the original evidence to decide whether a result answers your question before using it to choose a part.

item.title: 32 GB vs 64 GB RAM: decide from the work your PC actually does
item.description: Choose capacity from the applications, projects and multitasking you need, then check the exact platform and kit. Doubling RAM capacity does not promise double performance. Keep a working 32 GB setup unless a documented requirement or repeatable capacity problem supports the change.

item.title: Which PC parts can you reuse? A keep, replace and verify checklist
item.description: Reuse a component when its exact identity, condition and requirements suit the next complete PC. Start with an inventory, protect your data and check the dependencies. A part being old is not a reason to replace it; a part already owned is not automatic proof that it fits.

item.title: Plan a gaming and streaming PC around the stream you want to make
item.description: Test the game, capture scene, encoder and network together before choosing an upgrade. Streaming adds more than an encoding job, and a stream problem is not automatically a slow GPU. Start with the actual output you need and separate rendering, encoding and connection problems.

item.title: Plan a video-editing PC from your projects, not a gaming label
item.description: Record the editor version, source media, effects, output and working-storage needs before choosing parts. A requirements list can establish support; it cannot predict your timeline or export speed. Use a small representative project to identify the work the next PC needs to improve.

item.title: Plan a compact PC with a realistic noise goal
item.description: Choose a small PC layout, check shared GPU and cooler space, and plan repeatable noise checks without mistaking fit for cooling performance.

item.title: What to check before buying used PC parts
item.description: Check exact model identity, condition evidence, warranty terms, missing accessories and the complete cost before buying a used GPU or other PC component.

item.title: Air cooler or AIO for a Ryzen 7 7800X3D in the original North?
item.description: Compare NH-U12A and Liquid Freezer III 240 fit checks for a Ryzen 7 7800X3D in the original Fractal North, with layout conditions kept explicit.

item.title: RTX 3060 upgrade options: when to keep the card
item.description: Start with your exact RTX 3060 variant and actual games, then compare keeping it with documented GPU candidates and the complete cost of changing.
